title: Convergence proof assumes discriminator reaches optimum
description: The convergence result assumes that at each step the discriminator is allowed to reach its optimum given G before the generator distribution is updated.
canonical_description: convergence proof requires discriminator to reach optimum before each generator update

evidence.anchor: the discriminator is allowed to reach its optimum
evidence.quote: If $G$ and $D$ have enough capacity, and at each step of Algorithm~[REF:alg:AGF], the discriminator is allowed to reach its optimum given $G$, and $p_g$ is updated so as to improve the criterion $$\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x} \sim p_\text{data}}[\log D^*_G(\bm{x})] + \mathbb{E}_{\bm{x} \sim p_g}[\log (1 - D^*_G(\bm{x}))]$$ then $p_g$ converges to $p_\text{data}$

verdict.reasoning: Several papers directly remove the flagged assumption — that the discriminator must reach its optimum before each generator update — but only in restricted settings, so the general convergence question remains open. The pairwise-discriminator work shows that a redesigned objective can preserve alignment regardless of discriminator optimality and gives local convergence under a "sufficient discriminators" Hessian condition, yet explicitly defers global/joint convergence. The gradient descent-ascent analyses (both the local GDA linearization for isolated points with a kernel discriminator and the two-timescale GDA complexity results) prove convergence with single-step or two-timescale updates that never solve the inner max to optimality, but they are confined to local, stylized, or nonconvex-concave settings rather than general nonconvex-nonconcave GAN objectives. The first-order-limitations paper is important counter-evidence: it proves convergence only when the discriminator is set to its exact argmax each step and shows first-order dynamics can fail to converge in a simple mixture model, underscoring that no general convergence guarantee without the optimality assumption has been established. The zero-centered gradient penalty paper inherits only a narrow Dirac-GAN local guarantee. Thus the core assumption has been bypassed in specific frameworks, but a general convergence proof for realistic GANs without per-step discriminator optimality is still missing.

paper.title: On the Limitations of First-Order Approximation in GAN Dynamics
paper.abstract: While Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) have demonstrated promising performance on multiple vision tasks, their learning dynamics are not yet well understood, both in theory and in practice. To address this issue, we study GAN dynamics in a simple yet rich parametric model that exhibits several of the common problematic convergence behaviors such as vanishing gradients, mode collapse, and diverging or oscillatory behavior. In spite of the non-convex nature of our model, we are able to perform a rigorous theoretical analysis of its convergence behavior. Our analysis reveals an interesting dichotomy: a GAN with an optimal discriminator provably converges, while first order approximations of the discriminator steps lead to unstable GAN dynamics and mode collapse. Our result suggests that using first order discriminator steps (the de-facto standard in most existing GAN setups) might be one of the factors that makes GAN training challenging in practice.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly interrogates the optimal-discriminator assumption that the gap flags, by defining a parametric GMM model (mixtures of two univariate Gaussians with interval discriminators implementing total variation) and rigorously comparing two dynamics. It proves global convergence for the "optimal discriminator dynamics" (discriminator set to its exact argmax each step before the generator update) and gives experiments plus the "discriminator collapse" mechanism showing that "first order dynamics" (simultaneous gradient steps on discriminator and generator) frequently fail to converge — mode collapse, oscillation, vanishing gradients — even with many discriminator steps or unrolling. This bears on the gap because it is exactly a study of what happens when the convergence-proof assumption (discriminator reaching its optimum before each generator update) is replaced by realistic first-order discriminator steps.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap is about the fact that convergence results require the discriminator to reach its optimum before each generator update; the open problem implied by the gap is to obtain/justify convergence without that unrealistic requirement. This paper does NOT remove or relax that assumption: its main convergence theorem is proven precisely for the optimal-discriminator dynamics (exact argmax over discriminators each iteration), i.e., it retains the very assumption the gap criticizes. For the realistic first-order discriminator dynamics (which do not reach the optimum), the paper supplies no convergence proof — only simulations showing non-convergence — so it cannot serve as a positive convergence result under the relaxed setting. Thus the specific open issue of proving or characterizing convergence when the discriminator is not fully optimized before generator updates remains unsolved in general; the paper only demonstrates failure modes for one narrow parametric class (mixtures of two univariate unit-variance Gaussians with TV/interval discriminators, and in the experiments without a proof).
evidence_snippets: Our analysis reveals an interesting dichotomy: a GAN with an optimal discriminator provably converges, while first order approximations of the discriminator steps lead to unstable GAN dynamics and mode collapse.

In particular, if we take optimal discriminator steps, the training dynamics provably converge. In contrast, we show experimentally that the dynamics often fail if we take first order discriminator steps.
We do not provide a proof of convergence for the first order dynamics, but we remark that in light of our simulation results, this is simply because the first order dynamics do not converge.

paper.title: The Benefits of Pairwise Discriminators for Adversarial Training
paper.abstract: Adversarial training methods typically align distributions by solving two-player games. However, in most current formulations, even if the generator aligns perfectly with data, a sub-optimal discriminator can still drive the two apart. Absent additional regularization, the instability can manifest itself as a never-ending game. In this paper, we introduce a family of objectives by leveraging pairwise discriminators, and show that only the generator needs to converge. The alignment, if achieved, would be preserved with any discriminator. We provide sufficient conditions for local convergence; characterize the capacity balance that should guide the discriminator and generator choices; and construct examples of minimally sufficient discriminators. Empirically, we illustrate the theory and the effectiveness of our approach on synthetic examples. Moreover, we show that practical methods derived from our approach can better generate higher-resolution images.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly targets the gap's specific problem: it argues that with standard unary discriminators "generator can achieve alignment if and only if the discriminator reaches its optimum at the same time," and it redesigns the adversarial objective with pairwise discriminators (generator loss (p−q)^T A_D^g (p−q), i.e., g2 = −g1) so that the generator gradient at alignment q = p vanishes for every discriminator. Alignment is therefore preserved regardless of discriminator optimality, and the paper's convergence analysis ("only the generator needs to converge") gives sufficient local conditions (Hessian positive-definite off the reparametrization manifold, formalized as "sufficient discriminators") that do not require the discriminator to reach its optimum before each generator update.
assessments.what_remains_open: The specific requirement "discriminator reaches optimum before each generator update" is removed at the objective level and for local convergence, but the paper does not fully solve the general convergence question without any assumption on the discriminator side. Its formal local-convergence proposition (Prop. local_conv) is stated with a fixed discriminator ψ0, extended only to ψ remaining inside the open set of "sufficient discriminators" satisfying the Hessian condition; no proof is given that the actual alternating discriminator updates keep ψ inside that set in general. Global/joint convergence guarantees are explicitly deferred: "We hypothesize that the observed effect opens the possibility to establish global convergence guarantees for PairGAN-Z ... We leave further analysis of this problem for future work." So a full (global, joint-dynamics) convergence proof not resting on any discriminator-side condition remains open, though the core conceptual flaw in the gap (D optimality per generator step) is addressed.
evidence_snippets: In other words, generator can achieve alignment if and only if the discriminator reaches its optimum at the same time.
Utilizing such pairwise discriminators, we identify a family of training objectives which ensures alignment stability even if the discriminator is sub-optimal.

We note that in game [REF:eq:bgan_v1], since the generator loss is designed to preserve alignment once achieved, we only require the generator to reach alignment but do not require the discriminator to converge to a specific position.

paper.title: Local Convergence of Gradient Descent-Ascent for Training Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are a popular formulation to train generative models for complex high dimensional data. The standard method for training GANs involves a gradient descent-ascent (GDA) procedure on a minimax optimization problem. This procedure is hard to analyze in general due to the nonlinear nature of the dynamics. We study the local dynamics of GDA for training a GAN with a kernel-based discriminator. This convergence analysis is based on a linearization of a non-linear dynamical system that describes the GDA iterations, under an \textit{isolated points model} assumption from [Becker et al. 2022]. Our analysis brings out the effect of the learning rates, regularization, and the bandwidth of the kernel discriminator, on the local convergence rate of GDA. Importantly, we show phase transitions that indicate when the system converges, oscillates, or diverges. We also provide numerical simulations that verify our claims.

assessments.contribution_summary: This paper analyzes convergence of GAN training under the actual gradient descent-ascent (GDA) procedure in which the discriminator and generator each take a single gradient step per iteration, rather than assuming the discriminator is trained to optimality before each generator update. It linearizes the coupled, non-linear GDA dynamics around an equilibrium in an isolated-points model with an RBF/kernel discriminator, derives the Jacobian spectrum in terms of learning rates (η_d, η_g), regularization (λ), and kernel width (σ), and gives local stability conditions and explicit convergence rates (spectral radius < 1) together with phase transitions between convergence, oscillation, and divergence. Thus its convergence proof does not require discriminator optimality, directly addressing the gap.
assessments.what_remains_open: Regarding the narrow gap (requiring the discriminator to reach its optimum before each generator update), this paper fully avoids that assumption by analyzing single-step GDA dynamics. What remains open is generality: the analysis is local (asymptotic stability of a linearization around an equilibrium), restricted to a stylized setting of separated point masses ("isolated points model"), an RKHS/kernel (RBF) discriminator, equal generated-point weights, and equilibrium points coinciding with true samples; it does not provide global convergence guarantees, nor coverage of general/neural discriminators or non-separated data. Within those stylized conditions, however, the discriminator-optimality assumption is not part of the convergence proof.
evidence_snippets: In practice, however, we apply GDA for training GANs, whereby the discriminator is not allowed to converge, making analysis of the iterative training extremely difficult.
We assume the generator performs gradient descent on the above minimax optimization problem with a step size $\eta_g$ and the discriminator performs gradient ascent with step size $\eta_d$.
A well-known result of non-linear systems theory [CITE:vidyasagar2002nonlinear] is that the equilibrium point $(f_i^{*},\Xt_i^*)$ is locally asymptotically stable if $\rhomax(\J^*_i)< 1$.

paper.title: Two-Timescale Gradient Descent Ascent Algorithms for Nonconvex Minimax Optimization
paper.abstract: We provide a unified analysis of two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TTGDA) for solving structured nonconvex minimax optimization problems in the form of $\min_\textbf{x} \max_{\textbf{y} \in Y} f(\textbf{x}, \textbf{y})$, where the objective function $f(\textbf{x}, \textbf{y})$ is nonconvex in $\textbf{x}$ and concave in $\textbf{y}$, and the constraint set $Y \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is convex and bounded. In the convex-concave setting, the single-timescale gradient descent ascent (GDA) algorithm is widely used in applications and has been shown to have strong convergence guarantees. In more general settings, however, it can fail to converge. Our contribution is to design TTGDA algorithms that are effective beyond the convex-concave setting, efficiently finding a stationary point of the function $Φ(\cdot) := \max_{\textbf{y} \in Y} f(\cdot, \textbf{y})$. We also establish theoretical bounds on the complexity of solving both smooth and nonsmooth nonconvex-concave minimax optimization problems. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first systematic analysis of TTGDA for nonconvex minimax optimization, shedding light on its superior performance in training generative adversarial networks (GANs) and in other real-world application problems.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper analyzes two-timescale gradient descent ascent (TTGDA) and its stochastic variant TTSGDA, which are single-loop algorithms that update the min variable (generator) and max variable (discriminator) with one gradient step each per iteration — never requiring the inner max problem to be solved to its optimum before updating the min variable. It proves nonasymptotic ε-stationary-point complexity bounds for smooth and nonsmooth nonconvex-concave minimax problems, and explicitly motivates its proof technique as an alternative to nested-loop analyses that require y_t ≈ y*(x_t) at every step. This directly bears on the gap: it supplies convergence guarantees for a GAN-relevant (nonconvex-concave) class without assuming the discriminator/max-player reaches its optimum before each generator update.
assessments.what_remains_open: The gap's assumption is removed only within nonconvex-concave minimax problems, i.e., f is concave in the max variable (the discriminator-side problem) over a convex bounded set; genuine GAN objectives, which are nonconvex-nonconcave in general, are not covered — the paper itself notes it is NP-hard to determine whether an approximate min-max point exists in the general smooth nonconvex-nonconcave setting. Moreover, the established guarantees are average/visit-type ε-stationarity of Φ (Moreau-envelope based), not last-iterate convergence or saddle-point/Nash convergence for arbitrary GAN training. Thus the paper fully resolves the specific issue (no inner-optimality requirement) for the structured class it studies, while the broad GAN nonconvex-nonconcave case remains open.
evidence_snippets: Indeed, the previous frameworks are based on inexact gradient descent algorithms for minimizing a function $\Phi(\cdot) = \max_{\y \in \YCal} f(\cdot, \y)$, where a subroutine is designed for the inner problem of $\max_{\y \in \YCal} f(\x, \y)$ and which requires $\y_t$ to be close to $\y^\star(\x_t) = \argmax_{\y \in \YCal} f(\x_t, \y)$ at each iteration.
In order to overcome this issue, we have developed a new proof technique that directly analyzes the concave optimization problem with a slowly changing objective function.

The algorithm, referred to as gradient descent ascent (GDA), performs one-step gradient descent over the min variable $\x$ with a learning rate $\eta_\x > 0$ and one-step gradient ascent over the max variable $\y$ with another learning rate $\eta_\y > 0$.

paper.title: Improving Generalization and Stability of Generative Adversarial Networks
paper.abstract: Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) are one of the most popular tools for learning complex high dimensional distributions. However, generalization properties of GANs have not been well understood. In this paper, we analyze the generalization of GANs in practical settings. We show that discriminators trained on discrete datasets with the original GAN loss have poor generalization capability and do not approximate the theoretically optimal discriminator. We propose a zero-centered gradient penalty for improving the generalization of the discriminator by pushing it toward the optimal discriminator. The penalty guarantees the generalization and convergence of GANs. Experiments on synthetic and large scale datasets verify our theoretical analysis.

assessments.contribution_summary: The paper directly acknowledges the gap's premise — that the classical GAN convergence result requires the discriminator to be optimal at every step — and argues this condition is unrealistic because empirical discriminators trained on finite discrete datasets overfit and do not approximate the theoretically optimal discriminator. It then proposes a zero-centered gradient penalty (0-GP) that pushes empirical discriminators toward the optimal one, and claims convergence guarantees for 0-GP by inheriting the convergence of the 0-GP-sample penalty from prior Dirac-GAN analysis (Mescheder et al.), which is a gradient-based (not per-step-optimal-discriminator) convergence result. It also analyzes that fixed-ratio alternating gradient descent cannot maintain discriminator optimality, whereas TTUR potentially can.
assessments.what_remains_open: The paper does not provide a general convergence proof for GANs that removes the assumption that the discriminator reaches its optimum before each generator update. Its convergence guarantee is inherited from the Dirac GAN analysis of 0-GP-sample — a 1-D linear special case with local (near-equilibrium, oscillation-prevention) arguments — and it is not shown to hold for general distributions under realistic fixed/alternating update schedules. For TTUR the paper only states the discriminator "might be able to maintain its optimality," which still leaves open the core theoretical question of convergence when the optimal-discriminator-per-update condition is not satisfied in general settings.
evidence_snippets: One important result of the original paper is that, if the discriminator is optimal at every step of the GAN algorithm, then $p_g$ converges to $p_r$.

Alternating gradient descent with the same learning rate for discriminator and generator, and fixed number of discriminator updates per generator update (Fixed-Alt-GD) cannot maintain the (empirical) optimality of the discriminator.

Our GP forces the gradient w.r.t. all datapoints on the line segment between a pair of samples (including the two endpoints) to be $\bm 0$. As a result, our GP also prevents the generator from oscillating. Therefore, our GP has the same convergence guarantee as the 0-GP-sample.

ranking.feasibility_reasoning: This is a pure-theory gap, so data collection and compute are not barriers, and evaluability is clear (a theorem with stated assumptions either holds or not). The main feasibility problem is methodological maturity and scope: a fully general convergence proof for realistic (nonconvex-nonconcave) GAN training without per-step discriminator optimality is a hard open problem with known negative results showing first-order dynamics can fail even in simple mixtures. Existing progress is confined to local/stylized settings, two-timescale GDA, or redesigned objectives with extra conditions, so a small team can plausibly make incremental progress by extending these restricted analyses or proving new sufficient conditions. But closing the general gap as stated likely requires a fundamental advance in nonconvex-nonconcave minimax optimization, and 'realistic GANs' is a sprawling, ill-defined target.
